title: Cities: Skylines | Power, Politics, & Planning: Episode 1: Parking
premise: The presenter uses three increasingly destructive Cities: Skylines parking builds to argue that generous municipal parking minimums consume land, displace neighbors, raise development costs, and create politically persistent parking complaints despite abundant off-street supply.
coverage: Read complete machine ASR; inspected all 23 indexed contact sheets and all 265 frames, from 0 to 805 seconds, in the complete 809.968-second source. Index sampling is first available frame per 5-second bin plus scene score >0.30 at 480px width. Read native targeted stills at 215, 229.7, 230, 365, 645, and 805 seconds. Full speech is source-derived by the shared renderer from every timestamped transcript word, not authored excerpts. Panel boundaries group narrative rather than assert exact edit onset. Historical/policy assertions remain presenter claims. No source audio listening; sound arrays [] mean unannotated, not silence. Metadata credits Brahms intro music but its cue timing was not verified. Sparse images cannot guarantee every brief gag, insert, or soundtrack effect; changing sampled angles establish reframing/orbit only to the stated limits.

panels.heading: Opening identity and disproportionate parking
panels.description: A white title card displays the series name, blue Cities: Skylines bird, and ep. 1: PARKING, following aerial views of the office and its huge lot.
panels.camera: Opening sampled views change angle around the lot (frames 1–3), then cut to a static graphic (frames 4–5). Exact motion between samples is not established.
panels.action: Static title graphic; no visible character action.
panels.notes: The metadata credits Brahms Tragic Overture, Op. 81 (Musopen Symphony) as intro music; sound has not been source-listened or timed. ASR first segment spans an opening non-speech gap before Franklin at 24.61 seconds.

panels.heading: Franklin gives way to a modern planning series
panels.description: The office faces a broad divided road; PARKING appears in white over the game view as the presenter promises realistic lots and explains why they are dumb.
panels.camera: Largely fixed elevated frontal framing in frames 6–14; road vehicles change position.
panels.action: The game city remains running beneath the topic label.
panels.visualGag: Setup for the episode-wide irony: this ordinary-looking office tutorial will reveal parking land consumption rather than simply celebrate a realistic build.

panels.heading: Rule of thumb—not a real-life recommendation
panels.description: Black card: RULE OF THUMB (FOR CITIES: SKYLINES, NOT REAL LIFE), x amount parking per unit of floor area, .75 < x < 2.
panels.camera: Static card; successive text additions in frames 15–19.
panels.action: On-screen formula builds up; no human action.
panels.notes: The explicit visual qualification prevents mistaking the game heuristic for a recommended real-world regulation.

panels.heading: Case 1: cubicle farm on a greenfield site
panels.description: CASE 1: SUBURBAN OFFICE labels a lone dark office tower beside roads and vacant green land.
panels.camera: The elevated game viewpoint rotates around the office across frames 20–24; smoothness/speed cannot be established from still samples.
panels.action: No demolition yet; building and open site establish the demonstration.
panels.visualGag: Connected Case 1 setup: the cubicle-farm/spreadsheet-mine description and modest footprint will be contrasted with the parking acreage.

panels.heading: Measuring with whole office buildings
panels.description: Identical office copies fill a rectangular bank of roofs next to the original building, with a selected copy highlighted blue.
panels.camera: Framing becomes more overhead across frames 25–29; angle and scale change as copies are placed.
panels.action: Game editing duplicates the building to measure cumulative floor area.
panels.visualGag: Case 1 visual escalation: full office buildings become rulers for the much larger parking footprint. The later empty lot is the payoff.

panels.heading: Delete the measuring buildings
panels.description: One office survives while an enormous path outline and demolition dust replace the bank of copies.
panels.camera: Overhead views reorient across frames 30–36; a pale tool/traffic overlay alternates with the normal view.
panels.action: The copies are bulldozed; paths preserve their collective footprint.
panels.visualGag: Case 1 continuation: the extravagant bank of buildings disappears only to reserve the same land for cars, setting up the finished-lot contrast.

panels.heading: Asphalt and parking rows consume the outline
panels.description: Long rows of white parking lines are selected on the dark paved lot.
panels.camera: Views move from wide overhead site framing (37–42) to close parking-row views (43–46); a zoom/reframe is supported, continuous trajectory is not.
panels.action: The editor lays pavement and repeated parking-space assets.
panels.visualGag: Case 1 continuation: the land formerly represented by multiple towers becomes repeated car-storage rows.

panels.heading: Accessible spaces are not optional
panels.description: Three blue wheelchair-marked spaces with striped access aisles sit along the lot edge.
panels.camera: Close overhead framing shifts from regular rows to accessible spaces across frames 45–47.
panels.action: Accessible-space assets are placed.
panels.visualGag: Spoken mock-enforcement is visually anchored by the actual accessible stalls: the presenter threatens to find out if viewers omit them, while sincerely defending accessibility.
panels.notes: No disabled person or simulated inability to enter is shown; that is the narration’s hypothetical.

panels.heading: The lot gets landscaped
panels.description: Trees and planted islands appear near the office and arterial, with the brush and asset menus visible.
panels.camera: Changing close oblique/overhead angles across frames 48–53.
panels.action: The editor places trees and roadside details.
panels.visualGag: Setup for the sad-benches sequence: cosmetic amenities accompany the enormous paved site rather than solving the office-worker misery narrated next.

panels.heading: Sad benches and the tuna-salad lunch
panels.description: Repeated empty dark benches line a paved path among trees; the prop menu is searched for bench.
panels.camera: The view closes in on the path, pulls out briefly, then returns to the benches across frames 54–61. Sampled reframing does not prove one continuous move.
panels.action: Bench props are placed; no seated worker is visible.
panels.visualGag: Payoff to landscaping setup: the visible benches stage the narrator’s extended sad-lunch fantasy. The boss, sandwich, and personal insults exist only in speech.
panels.notes: Native 215-second still resolves the benches. The narrator continues the same imagined lunch/boss scenario into the next detailing view.

panels.heading: Back to harmless-looking flowers
panels.description: Small flowering plants and a fountain occupy the office frontage after the bench placement.
panels.camera: Close overhead view of planting (62–63), then wider frontal view at 64.
panels.action: The editor places a red-flowering tree/plant near the fountain.
panels.visualGag: End of the sad-benches sequence: the visual tutorial blandly resumes planting after the narrated workplace nightmare.
panels.notes: Native stills 229.7 and 230 seconds resolve the translucent rectangle as a flower-tree asset tooltip, not an insert of hands or a separate visual gag.

panels.heading: Huge finished lot—and still too little parking
panels.description: A UI-free aerial view shows the completed almost-empty lot dwarfing its office building.
panels.camera: Orbit/reframing around office and lot across frames 64–74; façade close-up at 67–68, pullback at 69, and changing aerial angles afterward.
panels.action: Completed-building showcase; ordinary road traffic remains visible in some views.
panels.visualGag: Case 1 payoff: the carefully landscaped sea of stalls looks excessive, yet the presenter says 244 spaces barely cover an implausibly small office population.

panels.heading: Case 2: a rehab inside an existing neighborhood
panels.description: CASE 2: LARGE REHAB appears over a warehouse-sized building amid continuous rows of homes and storefronts.
panels.camera: Cut from office showcase to new neighborhood; elevated camera rotates/reframes around rehab across frames 76–80.
panels.action: Existing buildings establish what the coming garage will displace.
panels.visualGag: Setup for Case 2 demolition/win-win irony: this is occupied urban fabric, unlike the first greenfield site.

panels.heading: A garage solves the arithmetic
panels.description: An isolated parking structure is shown with 4 x 7 x 4 = 112, exceeding the rehab’s narrated 84-block need.
panels.camera: Cut to open land at 81, then closer elevated angles around garage across 83–88.
panels.action: Garage and its access road are placed and examined.
panels.visualGag: Case 2 continuation: an efficient-looking vertical parking solution is prepared before its destructive neighborhood placement.

panels.heading: Searching for the least destructive placement
panels.description: A blue ghost parking garage is trial-positioned over buildings beside the rehab.
panels.camera: Cut back to neighborhood; top-down viewpoint rotates abruptly across frames 89–102. These are sampled editor reframings, not a proven continuous pan.
panels.action: The editor moves the garage preview through occupied parcels.
panels.visualGag: Case 2 setup sharpens the contradiction: least-destructive placement is visibly impossible without replacing neighbors.

panels.heading: Six houses and six apartments disappear
panels.description: Cleared ground opens beside the rehab; white captions list 6 ROWHOUSES and 6 SMALL APARTMENT BUILDINGS.
panels.camera: Elevated views reorient around the selected garage footprint across frames 103–108.
panels.action: Buildings are bulldozed; dust and warning markers mark the clearing.
panels.visualGag: Case 2 escalation: the on-screen demolition tally gives the sarcastic parking-for-everyone claim its human cost, completed by the next panel’s smiling game feedback.

panels.heading: Displacement earns smiling game feedback
panels.description: The placed garage fills the gap; captions add 6 BUSINESSES & 20–30 FAMILIES, while bright green smiling icons appear across surrounding buildings.
panels.camera: Rapid angle changes/pullback are visible across closely spaced frames 109–120, followed by a cut to storefront views at 121.
panels.action: The garage is committed and neighborhood feedback icons pop up.
panels.visualGag: Case 2 actual visual payoff: green smiles visually celebrate the placement against an explicit tally of destroyed homes, shops, and displaced families; the narration calls it worth it.
panels.notes: Native 365-second still confirms the tally and smile icons. Icons are game feedback, not observed happiness of displaced people.

panels.heading: A win-win for everyone except the losers
panels.description: Beauty views show storefronts, the rehab, and its adjoining new garage amid remaining row houses.
panels.camera: Cuts/reframings to low storefront views (121–122), then orbit/pullback around rehab (123–126).
panels.action: Completed neighborhood showcase; vehicle positions change.
panels.visualGag: Connected Case 2 payoff: respectable showcase imagery accompanies livelihoods ruined and win-win for everyone. The loss/green-smile irony belongs to this same sequence, not an unrelated gag.
panels.notes: The transcript mentions dumpster space; this selected wide frame does not resolve individual dumpsters. Later detailing shows bins and debris beside the garage.

panels.heading: Case 3: the small hotel rehab
panels.description: CASE 3: SMALL REHAB labels a narrow corner building with exterior fire escapes and a roof sign in a dense block.
panels.camera: Cut to new corner site; elevated viewpoint rotates across frames 127–132.
panels.action: Existing hotel and neighboring storefronts establish the next development.
panels.visualGag: Setup for the recurring demolition-for-parking gag: this small project will repeat the supposedly justified loss of its neighbors.

panels.heading: Twelve parking blocks for an L-shaped hotel
panels.description: A formula (2 x 2 x 4) - 4 = 12 overlays the corner hotel and neighboring shops.
panels.camera: Close elevated view changes angle/tilt toward overhead across frames 133–143; exact continuous camera path is not established.
panels.action: Buildings are selected/highlighted while parking demand is calculated.
panels.visualGag: Case 3 continuation: modest dimensional arithmetic sets up a far larger social price paid by adjacent homes and shops.
panels.notes: The four-block deduction is written on screen; the narrator explains the unoccupied quadrant of the L-shaped footprint.

panels.heading: Neighboring shops give way to asphalt
panels.description: Small neighboring buildings are removed; a paved strip is previewed across the gap behind/beside the hotel.
panels.camera: View pulls back for demolition (144–145), then closes in on pavement/lot across 146–149.
panels.action: Bulldozing and pavement/stall placement replace built parcels.
panels.visualGag: Case 3 escalation: a tiny luxury-conversion project visibly spreads into surrounding parcels, repeating Case 2’s parking-first logic.

panels.heading: A loading dock is the bonus
panels.description: A fenced paved enclosure with a truck is placed beside the hotel, adjoining the surface lot.
panels.camera: Close view on enclosure (150), changing angle to the rear (151), then overhead lot framing (152–153).
panels.action: Fence, loading-area truck prop, and parking details are placed.
panels.visualGag: Case 3 continuation: the pleasant extra amenity is obtained on land cleared of businesses and families; vehicle convenience is staged as the supposed benefit.
panels.notes: Truck is visibly an editor-selected prop; loading motion is not demonstrated.

panels.heading: The bargain: 34 spaces instead of neighbors
panels.description: Finished elevated view displays the hotel, adjacent surface lot, and fenced loading enclosure.
panels.camera: Changing clean showcase angles across frames 154–158, with a cut to neighboring storefronts at 157.
panels.action: Completed-lot showcase; road traffic remains visible.
panels.visualGag: Case 3 payoff: completely worth it celebrates eighteen condo spaces and sixteen shop spaces at the narrated cost of four businesses and ten families. Minor parking/loading inconvenience becomes the mock villain.
panels.notes: No casualty-count overlay was observed for this case. The displacement numbers come from narration.

panels.heading: The game demolition cuts to Tulsa
panels.description: After a brief replay of office-copy demolition, an aerial photograph shows wide parking lots around relatively isolated downtown buildings.
panels.camera: Hard change from gameplay to static aerial photograph by frame 164; photograph holds at 165.
panels.action: Static insert, no visible human action.
panels.notes: Tulsa identification is supplied by the presenter in this sequence; no independent image geolocation was performed.

panels.heading: New Haven: parking beside rail lines
panels.description: Static aerial image shows a station/rail corridor with large parking areas and surrounding development.
panels.camera: Cut to a different static aerial image at frame 166; no pan or zoom established.
panels.action: Static photograph.
panels.notes: Narration identifies New Haven, Connecticut; photograph is not independently geolocated.

panels.heading: Detroit: the actual parking landscape
panels.description: An aerial image shows a downtown grid containing large surface lots between buildings.
panels.camera: Cut to third static aerial photo at frame 168; it holds through 169.
panels.action: Static photograph.
panels.notes: Narration identifies Detroit, Michigan. These inserts escalate the policy argument, not a discovered separate gag.

panels.heading: Shoup supplies the explanatory frame
panels.description: The High Cost of Free Parking cover, naming Donald Shoup, overlays blurred/replayed parking construction.
panels.camera: Return to gameplay by frame 170; cut/overlay to static cover at 177.
panels.action: Repeated game lot construction under the book insert.
panels.notes: Book title and author spelling are supported by metadata and visible cover. Historical/policy statements remain attributed to presenter.

panels.heading: The costs of free parking accumulate
panels.description: White list over gameplay: LITTLE TO NO INCOME, USES HUGE AMOUNT OF SPACE, PRODUCES STORMWATER RUNOFF, PROVIDES LITTLE TAX REVENUE, DOES NOT SERVE NON-PARKERS.
panels.camera: Successive overhead lot views/reframings across frames 179–185; explanatory text remains fixed as lines accumulate.
panels.action: Lot-building footage repeats beneath the cost list.
panels.notes: The pictured parking area illustrates the presenter’s assertions; the sheet does not independently verify runoff or tax outcomes.

panels.heading: Different uses, different mandatory spaces
panels.description: A white code-example list overlays the office lot: worker, square footage, bedroom, hospital bed, and bowling lane requirements.
panels.camera: Gameplay shifts between overhead and close oblique views across frames 186–197; fixed white lines accumulate.
panels.action: Office frontage/lot editing continues beneath captions.
panels.notes: The presenter attributes inconsistent requirements to municipal copying rather than local studies; this is not an independent code audit.

panels.heading: The condos return as an overparking example
panels.description: The small rehab, loading enclosure, and parking strip reappear in a completed view with surrounding trucks and cars.
panels.camera: Cut back to hotel by frame 200; angle changes between frames 200–202.
panels.action: Vehicles change position on surrounding roads; buildings remain fixed.
panels.visualGag: Callback to Case 3’s bargain: the visible little condo project carries eighteen residential spaces plus commercial parking, making the earlier sarcastic payoff legible again.

panels.heading: Black Friday is still mostly empty
panels.description: Dan Gilmartin’s tweet shows a mostly empty lot and says Another enormous, 3/4 empty parking lot on #BlackFridayParking. Parking minimums are killing cities.
panels.camera: Game office footage continues behind a static centered tweet insert from frame 208 through 210. No photo motion established.
panels.action: Static tweet overlay and photograph.
panels.visualGag: Visual irony: worst-case shopping demand is invoked, then the inserted Black Friday photograph shows unused capacity instead of a full lot.
panels.notes: Native 645-second still resolves author @DPGilmartin and date 27 Nov 2015. Occupancy claim belongs to the tweet, not a new measurement here.

panels.heading: Parking podiums raise the cost of construction
panels.description: A low-angle photograph shows towers with tall slotted lower façades; a neighboring façade and cropped shop lettering remain in foreground.
panels.camera: Cut from gameplay to static architectural photograph at 214; holds at 215, then returns to gameplay at 216.
panels.action: Static photo illustration; no character action.
panels.notes: Narration identifies the function as parking podiums. Specific building names/location are unresolved; no name inferred from cropped lettering.

panels.heading: Rehabs can require demolition or never happen
panels.description: The large rehab and adjoining garage return in completed neighborhood views, illustrating how a change of use alters parking obligations.
panels.camera: Game detailing at 216–218, then cut to rehab at 219 and orbit/pullback through 222.
panels.action: Repeated completed-site showcase and editor detailing.
panels.visualGag: Callback to the Case 2 demolition/win-win sequence: the now-respectable finished project is shown while narration explains the parking obligations behind the destruction.
panels.notes: These are reprises, not evidence of a second separate demolition or independently verified development economics.

panels.heading: Parking governs development feasibility
panels.description: Benches and planted office paths recur as the presenter discusses parking costs, skyscraper feasibility, and minimums declining since their heyday.
panels.camera: Cut to close office detailing at 223, reframing over benches/roof across 224–229.
panels.action: Props, plants, and benches are selected/placed.
panels.notes: The bench imagery recalls earlier landscaping but no new comic line/insert is independently established in this stretch.

panels.heading: Abundant garages, scarce cheap curb spaces
panels.description: Garage placement is replayed with its neighborhood smiling icons, followed by fence/service-area detailing beside the garage.
panels.camera: Cut to dense neighborhood at 230; overhead-to-oblique changes across 231–236, then closer garage-side views across 237–242.
panels.action: Repeated garage placement/feedback is followed by adding service-space props.
panels.visualGag: Visual callback to Case 2’s green-smile payoff: abundant off-street provision coexists with political complaints, while the placement reprise again exhibits the game’s celebratory response to a destructive intervention.
panels.notes: The replay belongs to the original garage story, not a new displacement. Distinguish literal feedback icons from residents’ actual views.

panels.heading: The burden remains while cars come everywhere
panels.description: The small hotel lot is rebuilt in reprise: pavement and parking rows appear in the cleared strip between buildings.
panels.camera: Cut to small site at 244, close lot/pavement views through 249, wider near-overhead at 251.
panels.action: Editor previews/places asphalt and repeated stall assets.
panels.visualGag: Final callback to Case 3 demolition-for-parking: the presenter’s heavy-vehicle refrain accompanies the same car-storage strip occupying former building parcels.
panels.notes: The narrator notes transit-adjacent reform; no rail station is shown here, and no such scene is inferred.

panels.heading: Improve parking in the game—and real life
panels.description: Close detailing of the hotel’s loading enclosure and surface lot leads to a wider view of the completed corner project.
panels.camera: Alternating close overhead service-area views (253–256) and higher lot views (257–260).
panels.action: Props and details are adjusted around the parking/loading area.
panels.visualGag: Connected final payoff to the three-case satire: the tutorial finishes polishing the very spaces whose real-world costs it has exposed, while asking viewers to reconsider parking outside the game.

panels.heading: Patron acknowledgments
panels.description: Black card reads My Patreons and lists Liam Anderson, Connie Finley, magissima, bsquicklehausen, @southhost, and Daniel Lott.
panels.camera: Hard cut to static credit card at 261; unchanged through 263.
panels.action: Static text; no character action.
panels.notes: Names transcribed from the image, not inferred from spoken ASR.

panels.heading: One fare: channel outro
panels.description: A gray token on black reads GOOD FOR / DNE / ONE FARE beneath a translucent diagonal red stripe.
panels.camera: Transition from credit card to token between 263–264; it brightens between 264 and 265. No rotation or zoom established from these samples.
panels.action: Outro emblem fades into view.
panels.notes: Native 805-second still resolves token lettering. No parking-specific punchline or sound cue is inferred from the emblem.
